questions.question: Why are special methods needed in developmental psychobiology?
options: Infants may not understand instructions or provide verbal reports
Brain structure cannot be studied non-invasively before adolescence
Young children do not produce measurable physiological responses
Behavioral measures cannot provide information about perception or attention during infancy
questions.feedback: Developmental methods must often infer internal processes from behavior, physiology, or brain signals because infants and young children cannot always follow instructions or report their experience.

questions.question: Which type of method uses observable actions as an index of perception, attention, learning, or memory?
options: Peripheral physiological methods
Behavioral methods
Neural recording methods
Neuroimaging methods
questions.feedback: Behavioral methods use observable responses such as looking, orienting, habituation, or head turning to infer internal processes.

questions.question: When a participant cannot verbally report what they perceive or remember, what can serve as the dependent variable?
options: The participant's chronological age
Only the anatomical structure of the brain
A measurable behavioral response
The experimenter's interpretation of the stimulus
questions.feedback: In developmental behavioral methods, measurable behavior can serve as the dependent variable.

questions.question: What is the orienting response?
options: A progressive decrease in response after many repetitions of one stimulus
A learned head turn reinforced by an interesting visual event
A preference for a familiar over a novel stimulus
A coordinated response to a novel or salient event
questions.feedback: The orienting response is a coordinated reaction to a novel or salient event and can include changes in gaze, head position, heart rate, or ongoing behavior.

questions.question: What is the basic logic of an expectancy-violation experiment?
options: Compare responses to expected and unexpected events
Reward a head turn after a change in sound
Repeat one stimulus until the response decreases
Average scalp electrical activity across repeated events
questions.feedback: Expectancy-violation paradigms compare responses to expected events with responses to unexpected or impossible events.

questions.question: Why must longer looking at an unexpected event be interpreted carefully?
options: Infants cannot reliably move their eyes during early development
Perceptual salience can also influence looking time
Unexpected events always produce identical looking responses
Looking time is unrelated to visual processing in infancy
questions.feedback: Longer looking can reflect expectancy violation, but perceptual salience can also affect looking time, so appropriate controls are necessary.

questions.question: What is habituation?
options: A conditioned movement learned through reinforcement
A progressive increase in response to repeated stimulation
Response reduction after repeated stimulation
An averaged EEG response to repeated events
questions.feedback: Habituation is the progressive reduction of a response when the same stimulus is presented repeatedly.

questions.question: What does recovery of responding to a new stimulus after habituation suggest?
options: The sensory modality has become temporarily insensitive to stimulation
The new stimulus was physically more intense than the old one
The habituated stimulus has been completely forgotten
The new stimulus was detected as different
questions.feedback: Recovery after habituation indicates that the new stimulus was discriminated from the habituated stimulus.

questions.question: What is conditioned head turning commonly used to test?
options: Auditory discrimination
Visual acuity
Cortical blood oxygenation
White-matter organization
questions.feedback: Once the conditioned response is learned, head turning can be used to test whether an infant detects a change in sound.

questions.question: What does preferential looking measure?
options: The speed of neural activity following an auditory event
Relative looking time between alternative visual stimuli
Pressure produced during sucking
Regional radioactive tracer uptake
questions.feedback: Preferential looking compares how long an infant looks at alternative visual stimuli.

questions.question: What do Teller acuity cards estimate?
options: Recognition memory
Heart-rate variability
Visual acuity
Auditory discrimination
questions.feedback: Teller acuity cards use preferential looking to estimate visual acuity in infants and other non-verbal participants.

questions.question: How are Teller acuity cards used to estimate visual acuity?
options: EEG is recorded while the infant views a uniform field
Tones of progressively increasing frequency are presented until detection fails
The infant presses a button whenever a striped grating becomes visible
Present increasingly fine gratings until orientation fails
questions.feedback: The finest grating that still produces reliable orientation provides an estimate of visual acuity.

questions.question: What is the Visual Paired Comparison task used to study?
options: Recognition memory
Cortical blood flow using near-infrared light
Neural oscillations using scalp electrodes
Motor control through reinforced head turning
questions.feedback: Visual Paired Comparison uses looking differences between familiar and novel stimuli to study recognition and memory.

questions.question: What is one advantage of peripheral physiological measures in developmental research?
options: They always identify the exact cognitive process responsible for a response
Useful when overt behavior is unavailable
They directly record action potentials from individual neurons in the brain
They provide more precise anatomical localization than structural MRI
questions.feedback: Peripheral physiological measures can reveal responses even when overt behavior is difficult to obtain or interpret.

questions.question: Why is heart-rate variability informative but not specific?
options: HRV can be measured only in adult participants
HRV cannot change during attention or arousal
HRV lacks cognitive specificity
Measuring HRV requires exposure to ionizing radiation
questions.feedback: HRV can change with attention or arousal, but the signal alone does not uniquely identify the underlying cognitive process.

questions.question: What is non-nutritive sucking?
options: A reflex that occurs only when food is delivered
A method for measuring electrical potentials from the scalp
A learned behavior that appears only after language develops
Spontaneous sucking on a pacifier or nipple without feeding
questions.feedback: Non-nutritive sucking is sucking that occurs without feeding and can be measured in very young infants.

questions.question: What is the core manipulation in the high-amplitude sucking paradigm?
options: Strong sucks trigger stimulus delivery
A head turn terminates the ongoing stimulus
Visual stimuli appear only after the infant looks away
Sounds are presented independently of the infant's sucking behavior
questions.feedback: In high-amplitude sucking, sufficiently strong sucks trigger a sound or another stimulus.

questions.question: What did Vouloumanos and Werker (2007) compare in newborns?
options: Responses to familiar and unfamiliar visual faces after repeated exposure
Speech and non-speech sounds using high-amplitude sucking
High- and low-spatial-frequency gratings
Speech before and after sleep
questions.feedback: Vouloumanos and Werker (2007) used high-amplitude sucking to compare newborn responses to speech and non-speech sounds.

questions.question: What response pattern did newborns show for speech and non-speech sounds in Vouloumanos and Werker (2007)?
options: Responses habituated equally quickly to both sound categories
Responses increased only for non-speech and disappeared for speech
Responses habituated to non-speech but remained higher or showed little habituation to speech
Responses were indistinguishable because newborns could not discriminate the sounds
questions.feedback: Newborn sucking responses progressively decreased for non-speech sounds, while responses to speech remained higher or showed little habituation.

questions.question: What methodological trade-off is illustrated by comparing EEG and fMRI?
options: Observable behavior versus explicit verbal self-report
Familiarity effects versus perceptual preference
Direct electromagnetic recording versus radioactive metabolic imaging
Temporal resolution versus spatial localization
questions.feedback: EEG has excellent temporal resolution but limited spatial localization, whereas fMRI provides better spatial localization but measures a slower hemodynamic response.

questions.question: What does electroencephalography (EEG) record?
options: Scalp electrical potential differences
Magnetic fields generated by neuronal electrical currents
Changes in near-infrared light absorption through cortical tissue
Regional accumulation of radioactive metabolic tracers
questions.feedback: EEG records differences in electrical potential using electrodes placed on the scalp.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of EEG in developmental research?
options: Detailed anatomical localization of deep brain structures
Millisecond timing during passive stimulation
Single-neuron action-potential recording through the intact scalp
High-resolution measurement of slow cerebral hemodynamic responses
questions.feedback: EEG is non-invasive, silent, suitable for passive stimulation, and has millisecond temporal resolution.

questions.question: What does scalp EEG mainly reflect?
options: Action potentials from individual neurons beneath each scalp electrode
Local cerebral blood-flow changes
Synchronized postsynaptic currents in cortical populations
Regional radioactive tracer decay
questions.feedback: Scalp EEG mainly reflects population-level electrical fields generated by synchronized postsynaptic currents, not individual spikes.

questions.question: Which EEG frequency band is approximately 8-13 Hz?
options: Delta
Beta
Gamma
Alpha
questions.feedback: The alpha frequency band is approximately 8-13 Hz.

questions.question: What does spectral analysis of spontaneous EEG do?
options: EEG frequency content
Cortical anatomy reconstructed from MRI
Arrival timing of gamma photons
Averaged activity locked to repeated events
questions.feedback: Spectral analysis quantifies how much EEG activity is present at different frequencies or frequency bands.

questions.question: How is an event-related potential (ERP) obtained?
options: By measuring spontaneous EEG without reference to event timing
By aligning EEG to repeated events and averaging across trials
By injecting a tracer and reconstructing its regional distribution
By applying a magnetic pulse and measuring its behavioral effect
questions.feedback: ERPs are obtained by aligning EEG activity to repeated events and averaging across trials.

questions.question: Why does averaging across trials help reveal an ERP?
options: It removes every low-frequency component from the EEG
It converts electrical activity into a hemodynamic response
It attenuates activity that is not consistently time-locked to the event
It amplifies activity that is unrelated to event timing
questions.feedback: Averaging emphasizes reproducible event-related activity while reducing activity that is not consistently time-locked.

questions.question: What does magnetoencephalography (MEG) measure?
options: Electrical potentials measured from the scalp
Changes in cerebral blood oxygenation
Gamma photons
Neuronal magnetic fields
questions.feedback: MEG measures the small magnetic fields produced by neuronal electrical currents.

questions.question: What makes fetal MEG useful for developmental research?
options: Non-invasive detection of fetal brain activity
Direct measurement of fetal neurotransmitter concentrations
Detailed structural imaging of developing fetal white-matter pathways
Measurement of fetal metabolism using radioactive tracers
questions.feedback: Fetal MEG can detect magnetic fields generated by the fetal brain through the maternal abdomen, allowing neural activity to be studied before birth.

questions.question: Which methods directly measure electromagnetic consequences of neural activity?
options: fMRI and fNIRS
EEG and MEG
PET and fMRI
TMS and structural MRI
questions.feedback: EEG and MEG directly measure electrical or magnetic signals generated by neural activity.

questions.question: Which methods primarily measure physiological consequences associated with neural activity rather than neural electrical activity itself?
options: EEG and MEG
TMS and EEG
fMRI, fNIRS, and PET
Conditioned head turning and EEG
questions.feedback: fMRI, fNIRS, and PET infer neural activity from physiological consequences such as blood oxygenation, blood flow, or metabolism.

questions.question: What is neurovascular coupling?
options: Conversion of scalp electrical potentials into magnetic fields generated outside the head
Reconstruction of positron-annihilation events from coincident gamma-photon detections
Reduction of a behavioral response after repeated exposure to one stimulus
Coupling between neural activity and local vascular responses
questions.feedback: Neurovascular coupling links changes in local neural activity to vascular changes including cerebral blood flow, blood volume, and hemoglobin oxygenation.

questions.question: What does diffusion MRI or DTI investigate?
options: White-matter pathway organization
Patterns of peripheral autonomic arousal
Auditory mismatch responses
Postsynaptic receptor clustering
questions.feedback: Diffusion MRI and DTI use the diffusion of water to investigate white-matter organization.

questions.question: What does BOLD stand for?
options: Blood-Optical Light Detection
Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent
Brain-Output Localization Difference
Brain-Oxygen-Level Distribution
questions.feedback: BOLD stands for Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent.

questions.question: What typically happens to deoxyhemoglobin during a positive BOLD response?
options: Deoxyhemoglobin concentration increases
Deoxyhemoglobin remains approximately constant
Deoxyhemoglobin decreases
Neurons convert deoxyhemoglobin directly into oxyhemoglobin
questions.feedback: During a typical positive BOLD response, the increase in cerebral blood flow exceeds the increase in oxygen consumption, reducing local deoxyhemoglobin concentration.

questions.question: Why is the BOLD signal considered an indirect measure of neural activity?
options: It measures magnetic fields generated directly by synchronized neuronal currents
It detects action potentials from individual neurons using scalp electrodes
It infers brain activity only from observable behavior
It measures vascular responses coupled to neural activity
questions.feedback: BOLD reflects hemodynamic changes coupled to neural activity rather than neuronal electrical activity itself.

questions.question: Why does fMRI have poorer temporal resolution than EEG or MEG?
options: The hemodynamic response develops over several seconds
MRI requires a verbal response from the participant
BOLD can measure only spontaneous resting activity
Magnetic resonance cannot detect oxygenation changes
questions.feedback: Neural events occur rapidly, but the hemodynamic response measured with fMRI unfolds over several seconds.

questions.question: What does functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) use to estimate cortical hemodynamic changes?
options: Scalp electrical potentials
Near-infrared light
Strong magnetic pulses
Radioactive tracers
questions.feedback: fNIRS uses near-infrared light delivered through the scalp to estimate changes in cortical hemoglobin concentrations.

questions.question: Which hemoglobin-related measures can fNIRS estimate?
options: Only oxygenated hemoglobin and cerebral blood flow
Only deoxygenated hemoglobin and blood volume
Oxygenated, deoxygenated, and total hemoglobin
Only total hemoglobin and arterial oxygen pressure
questions.feedback: fNIRS can estimate changes in oxygenated hemoglobin (OHb), deoxygenated hemoglobin (DHb), and total hemoglobin (THb).

questions.question: What does total hemoglobin (THb) represent in fNIRS?
options: Hemoglobin contained only in arterial blood
The difference between oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin
The amount of oxygen directly consumed by neurons
The sum of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin
questions.feedback: Total hemoglobin is the sum of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin and is related to local blood volume.

questions.question: What is an important advantage of fNIRS for developmental research?
options: Low-burden, silent testing in infants
Complete coverage of deep brain structures during natural behavior
Single-neuron recordings from superficial cortex
Spatial resolution exceeding structural MRI
questions.feedback: fNIRS has a relatively low experimental burden and can be used with infants, including during more naturalistic or social situations.

questions.question: What is an important limitation of fNIRS?
options: It always requires a large superconducting magnet
It is mainly sensitive to superficial cortical tissue
It cannot detect changes in hemoglobin concentration
It necessarily requires administration of a radioactive tracer
questions.feedback: A major limitation of fNIRS is that it mainly samples superficial cortex and is also sensitive to scalp blood flow and movement.

questions.question: What does positron emission tomography (PET) use to measure physiological processes?
options: Scalp electrical potentials
Magnetic fields from neuronal currents
Radioactive tracers whose regional distribution can be detected
Near-infrared light reflected from cortex
questions.feedback: PET uses radioactive tracers to measure physiological processes such as metabolism or receptor binding.

questions.question: What happens during positron-electron annihilation in PET?
options: The positron becomes an electrical potential at the scalp
A single infrared photon is emitted through the skull
The electron generates a magnetic pulse that stimulates cortex
Two gamma photons are emitted in approximately opposite directions
questions.feedback: Positron-electron annihilation produces two gamma photons emitted in approximately opposite directions.

questions.question: What does coincidence detection identify in PET?
options: A line of response between two detectors
The position of a TMS coil
The frequency of an EEG oscillation
The latency of an ERP component
questions.feedback: Nearly simultaneous detection of the two annihilation photons defines a line of response between detectors.

questions.question: Why is PET strongly limited in healthy developmental populations?
options: It requires a learned head-turn response
It exposes participants to ionizing radiation
It cannot provide spatial information
It cannot measure physiological processes
questions.feedback: PET requires radioactive tracers and therefore exposes participants to ionizing radiation, limiting its use in healthy children.

questions.question: How is transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) best classified?
options: A peripheral physiological recording method
A structural MRI technique
A cortical perturbation method
An indirect hemodynamic recording method
questions.feedback: TMS is primarily a perturbation method: it transiently changes neural activity rather than simply recording it.

questions.question: What physical principle allows TMS to influence cortical tissue?
options: Direct electrical injection from scalp electrodes into deep white matter
Gamma-photon emission from radioactive tracers placed in cortical tissue
Infrared depolarization of cortical neurons
Electromagnetic induction of cortical electric fields
questions.feedback: A rapidly changing magnetic field generated by the TMS coil induces an electric field in cortical tissue.

questions.question: What kind of inference can TMS strengthen compared with purely recording methods?
options: A causal inference about the contribution of a brain region
An estimate of visual acuity from preferential looking
An estimate of total hemoglobin concentration
A measure of spontaneous EEG frequency content
questions.feedback: Because TMS perturbs activity and allows the consequences to be measured, it can provide stronger evidence for a causal contribution of a stimulated region.

questions.question: What is the main distinction between recording and perturbation methods?
options: Recording methods are invasive, whereas perturbation methods are always non-invasive
Recording methods reveal associations, whereas perturbation methods can test causal contributions
Recording methods measure behavior, whereas perturbation methods measure anatomy
Recording methods are used only in adults, whereas perturbation methods are used only in infants
questions.feedback: Recording methods show that a neural signal is associated with a stimulus or behavior, whereas perturbation methods can test whether changing neural activity changes behavior.
